fields.Front: What does a sequence diagram show?
fields.Back: The flow of messages (method calls) between objects during a particular scenario or use case, over time as a sequence of events.

fields.Front: What are the four elements of a sequence diagram listed in the slides?
fields.Back: Actors (external entities), Objects/Participants, Messages (arrows), Conditions (control-flow structures like alt and loops).

fields.Front: In a sequence diagram, what is an alt fragment?
fields.Back: A frame for alternatives: divided into regions each guarded by a condition in brackets (e.g., [If card is valid]); exactly one region executes.

fields.Front: In which direction does time flow in a sequence diagram?

fields.Text: ATM sequence diagram nested alt guards, outer to inner: [If {{c1::card is valid}}], [If {{c2::PIN is valid}}], [If {{c3::funds are sufficient}}].

fields.Front: In the ATM sequence diagram, what happens when funds are sufficient?
fields.Back: BankAccount → BankServer: Funds OK; BankServer → ATM: Withdraw Amount; ATM → User: Dispense Cash; BankServer → ATM: Transaction Successful.

fields.Front: In the ATM sequence diagram, what happens in the [Insufficient funds] region?
fields.Back: BankAccount → BankServer: Insufficient Funds; BankServer → ATM: Transaction Unsuccessful; ATM → User: Eject Card.

fields.Front: What three modelling guidelines are given for sequence diagrams?
fields.Back: Clarity over completeness; iterative design; avoid pitfalls (too many classes, diagrams too detailed for the audience).

fields.Text: Sequence diagram pitfalls: {{c1::too many classes}} and making diagrams {{c2::too detailed for the audience}}.
In the ATM sequence diagram, the first message is User → ATM: {{c1::Insert Card}}, followed by ATM → BankServer: {{c2::Verify Card}}.
